sections.heading: 1. Conceptual Framework: Risk Factors vs. Prognostic Factors

blocks.text: Glaucoma is a multifactorial optic neuropathy in which distinct demographic, biometric, genetic, vascular, and ocular variables determine disease susceptibility [1]. In clinical epidemiology, **risk factors** are characteristics statistically associated with the *development* of glaucoma in previously unaffected individuals (as defined in ocular hypertension cohorts such as OHTS), whereas **prognostic factors** predict the *rate of progression* once glaucomatous optic neuropathy is established (as quantified in EMGT and AGIS) [1], [3].

Although **primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)** and **primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG)** both culminate in retinal ganglion cell apoptosis, their underlying anatomical and demographic risk profiles diverge sharply, making systematic risk stratification vital for population screening and individualized management [1], [2].

sections.heading: 2. Major Risk Factors for Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG)

blocks.text: A. Elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP)

Elevated IOP is the **strongest and only proven modifiable risk factor** for both the onset and progression of POAG [1], [3]. Rather than operating across a rigid cutoff at 21 mmHg, IOP exerts a continuous, dose-dependent effect: in the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS) and Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT), each **1 mmHg increase** in baseline IOP raised the risk of POAG development or progression by approximately **10%** [1], [3]. Wide diurnal fluctuations and elevated peak IOP further compound optic nerve vulnerability [2].
B. Demographic & Genetic Risk Factors

items: **Advancing Age:** POAG prevalence increases exponentially after age 40, rising from approximately 0.5–1% in the fifth decade to 4–8% in individuals older than 70–80 years, reflecting cumulative trabecular endothelial loss, extracellular matrix deposition, and age-related lamina cribrosa stiffening [1], [2].

**Race and Ethnicity:** Population studies including the **Baltimore Eye Survey** and **Barbados Eye Study** demonstrated that individuals of African or Afro-Caribbean descent have a **3–5 times higher prevalence** of POAG, develop disease roughly a decade earlier, present with greater structural severity, and suffer a 6–8 times higher risk of glaucoma blindness compared with European populations [1], [2]. Hispanic/Latino populations (Los Angeles Latino Eye Study) exhibit an intermediate-to-high prevalence approaching that of African Americans in older age strata [1].

**Family History and Genetics:** Having an affected first-degree relative confers a **4–9-fold increased risk** of developing POAG; in the **Rotterdam Study**, siblings of POAG patients carried a **9.2-fold lifetime risk**, stronger than the risk associated with an affected parent [2]. Monogenic mutations account for ~5% of POAG—most notably *MYOC* (myocilin/TIGR) in juvenile and high-tension POAG, and *OPTN* (optineurin) or *TBK1* duplications in familial normal-tension glaucoma (NTG)—while common polygenic risk loci include *CDKN2B-AS1*, *TMCO1*, *CAV1/CAV2*, and *SIX1/SIX6* [1], [2].

blocks.text: C. Ocular Structural & Refractive Risk Factors

items: **Thin Central Corneal Thickness (CCT):** OHTS identified thin CCT as a powerful independent predictor of conversion from ocular hypertension to POAG: eyes with **CCT ≤555 µm had a 3-fold greater risk** of developing POAG than eyes with CCT >588 µm (hazard ratio ~1.71 per 40 µm thinner CCT) [3]. Beyond causing Goldmann applanation tonometry to underestimate true IOP, a thin cornea may reflect generalized biomechanical fragility of the corneoscleral shell and lamina cribrosa [1], [3].

**Myopia:** Moderate-to-high myopia (typically > −3.00 D) increases POAG risk **2–3-fold** in population cohorts such as the **Blue Mountains Eye Study** and **Barbados Eye Study**, likely because axial elongation stretches and thins the lamina cribrosa and peripapillary sclera [1], [2].

**Optic Nerve Head Features:** Larger baseline **vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR)**, greater pattern standard deviation (PSD) on perimetry, **optic disc splinter (Drance) hemorrhages**, large optic disc area, and **beta-zone peripapillary atrophy (β-PPA)** significantly elevate the probability of POAG onset or progression [1], [3].

blocks.text: D. Vascular & Systemic Risk Factors

Low **ocular perfusion pressure (OPP)**—particularly **low diastolic OPP** (DOPP = DBP − IOP < 50–55 mmHg)—emerged as a consistent independent risk factor for POAG across the Baltimore, Barbados, and Egna–Neumarkt studies [1], [2]. Systemic hypotension (especially excessive nocturnal blood pressure dipping from overtreated hypertension), primary vascular dysregulation (migraine, Raynaud phenomenon, cold extremities—particularly prominent in NTG), and obstructive sleep apnea impair optic nerve head autoregulation [2]. Type 2 diabetes mellitus shows a modest positive association with POAG in large meta-analyses (despite an apparent protective artifact in OHTS Phase 1 that was not sustained upon longer follow-up), while long-term systemic or topical corticosteroid responsiveness precipitates secondary open-angle IOP elevation [1], [3].

sections.heading: 3. Major Risk Factors for Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG)

blocks.text: A. Demographic & Genetic Determinants

items: **Advancing Age:** PACG prevalence rises steadily after age 40 and peaks in the **6th to 7th decades** because the crystalline lens thickens continuously throughout life (~0.02 mm/year) and moves anteriorly, progressively narrowing the iridocorneal angle and intensifying relative pupillary block [1], [4].

**Female Sex:** Women have a **2–4-fold higher risk** of developing PACG than men across nearly all ethnic groups, reflecting anatomically shorter axial lengths, shallower anterior chambers, and narrower anterior chamber angles in female eyes [1], [4].

**Race and Ethnicity:** PACG demonstrates striking geographic clustering, with the highest prevalence among **Inuit/Eskimo** populations (2–4% in adults >40 years) and **East and South Asian** populations (Chinese, Mongolian, and Indian cohorts such as the **Chennai Glaucoma Study** and **APEDS**) [4]. More than **80% of individuals with PACG worldwide live in Asia**, and although POAG is more common globally, PACG causes a disproportionately high burden of bilateral blindness [1], [4].

**Family History and Heritability:** First-degree relatives of PACG patients have a **3.5–6 times higher risk** of occludable angles or angle closure, as key biometric determinants (anterior chamber depth and axial length) carry 70–90% heritability [2], [4]. Genome-wide association studies have identified susceptibility loci including *PLEKHA7*, *COL11A1*, *PCMTD1-ST18*, *EPDR1*, *CHAT*, and *GLIS3* [1], [4].

blocks.text: B. Static Ocular Biometric Risk Factors

items: **Shallow Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD) and Small AC Volume:** A central **ACD <2.5 mm** (and narrow peripheral angle) is the classic hallmark of an occludable eye, bringing the peripheral iris close to the trabecular meshwork [1], [4].

**Short Axial Length and Hypermetropia:** Hypermetropic eyes with **axial length <22.0–22.5 mm** possess a crowded anterior segment; extreme short eyes (**nanophthalmos**, AL <20.0 mm) carry an exceptionally high risk of severe angle closure and uveal effusion [2].

**Thick, Anteriorly Positioned Crystalline Lens & High Lens Vault:** Increased lens thickness (>4.5–5.0 mm), steeper anterior lens curvature, and greater **lens vault (LV)**—the perpendicular protrusion of the anterior lens pole anterior to the scleral spur plane on AS-OCT—represent the **strongest independent biometric predictor** of angle closure [4].
**Small Corneal Diameter and Steep Corneal Curvature:** A small anterior segment diameter reduces the available space within the iridocorneal recess [2].

**Iris and Ciliary Body Morphology:** A **thick peripheral iris**, an **anteriorly inserted iris root**, and **anteriorly positioned/rotated ciliary processes** (producing **plateau iris configuration**) cause direct non-pupillary-block angle crowding [1], [4].

blocks.text: C. Dynamic Physiological & Precipitating Risk Factors

Static biometry alone explains only a fraction of angle closure; dynamic physiological behavior differentiates eyes that actually close from anatomically similar eyes that remain open [4]. Normally, the spongy iris stroma loses fluid and **decreases in cross-sectional volume during pupil dilation**, whereas eyes predisposed to PACG retain iris volume during dilation, mechanically stuffing the peripheral angle [4]. In addition, dynamic **choroidal expansion** increases posterior segment volume and drives the lens–iris diaphragm anteriorly, further exacerbating pupillary block (Quigley's hypothesis) [4].

blocks.title: Precipitating Environmental & Pharmacologic Triggers for Acute Angle Closure
items: **Mid-Dilation (3–5 mm Pupil):** Dim ambient illumination (movie theaters, evening reading), emotional stress, or sympathetic surge maximizes iridolenticular contact and relative pupillary block [1].

**Medications:** Topical mydriatics/cycloplegics, systemic anticholinergics (antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, ipratropium, oxybutynin), and adrenergic decongestants precipitate pupillary-block angle closure; **topiramate** and sulfonamides induce **ciliochoroidal effusion** with forward lens–iris shift causing bilateral non-pupillary-block angle closure [1], [2].

sections.heading: 1. Targeted Clinical History & Systemic Risk Assessment

blocks.text: Evaluating a patient suspected of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) or primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) begins with a structured history designed to uncover occult visual loss, intermittent angle-closure episodes, secondary causes, and systemic contraindications to future therapy [1], [2].

items: **Ocular Symptoms:** POAG is classically **asymptomatic** until advanced paracentral or peripheral visual field loss develops, whereas angle-closure disease may present either silently (chronic PACG) or with **intermittent subacute attacks** (evening brow ache, colored halos around lights from corneal epithelial edema, transient blurring relieved by sleep-induced miosis) or **acute angle-closure crisis** (severe unilateral eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, red eye, and marked visual loss) [1], [4].

**Ocular & Medication History:** Document refractive error (myopia vs. hypermetropia), prior ocular trauma, uveitis, retinal vascular occlusions, laser/intraocular surgery, and exposure to **corticosteroids** (topical, periocular, intravitreal, inhaled, or oral) or angle-narrowing drugs (anticholinergics, adrenergics, **topiramate**) [1], [2].

**Systemic & Family History:** Elicit a family history of glaucoma or blindness in first-degree relatives, vascular risk factors (hypertension, nocturnal hypotension, migraine, Raynaud phenomenon, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea), and systemic comorbidities affecting medication safety—specifically **asthma/COPD, sinus bradycardia, or AV block** (beta-blocker contraindications) and **sulfonamide allergy or renal calculi** (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor precautions) [1], [4].

sections.heading: 2. Visual Function, Pupillary & Anterior Segment Examination

blocks.text: A meticulous anterior segment evaluation establishes baseline visual function, screens for anterior chamber shallowing, and actively excludes secondary glaucomas before any mydriatic drops are instilled [1], [2].

items: **Visual Acuity & Refraction:** Record best-corrected distance visual acuity (BCVA) and manifest refraction; high myopia raises suspicion for POAG or pigmentary glaucoma, whereas hypermetropia raises the pretest probability of angle closure [1].

**Pupillary Examination:** Perform the swinging flashlight test before dilation to detect a **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)**, a sensitive objective sign of asymmetric glaucomatous optic neuropathy (typically requires ≥30–50% asymmetric nerve fiber loss) [2]. In acute PAC, look for a **mid-dilated, vertically oval, sluggish or fixed pupil** caused by ischemic sphincter paralysis [4].

**Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy:** Inspect the conjunctiva for ciliary injection (acute PAC) or dilated episcleral veins; examine the cornea for microcystic epithelial edema, endothelial pigment (**Krukenberg spindle**), or keratic precipitates; evaluate anterior chamber clarity (cells/flare) and depth; inspect the iris for **sectoral spiral atrophy**, posterior synechiae, pseudoexfoliation flakes at the pupillary ruff, transillumination defects, or neovascularization (NVI); and assess the crystalline lens for **glaucomflecken** (anterior subcapsular necrotic opacities pathognomonic of prior acute IOP spike), phacomorphic intumescence, or pseudoexfoliation target sign [1], [4].

**Van Herick Peripheral AC Depth Screening:** Direct a narrow slit beam at 60° onto the peripheral temporal cornea just inside the limbus and compare peripheral AC depth to corneal thickness (CT): **Grade 4 (≥1 CT)** and **Grade 3 (1/2–1/4 CT)** indicate low closure risk, whereas **Grade 2 (1/4 CT)** and **Grade 1 (<1/4 CT)** indicate a potentially occludable angle [2]. Critically, Van Herick is purely a screening adjunct and **never replaces gonioscopy** [1], [2].

sections.heading: 3. Intraocular Pressure Measurement (Tonometry) & Pachymetry

blocks.text: **Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT)** remains the clinical reference standard for IOP measurement (based on the modified Imbert–Fick principle over a 3.06 mm applanation diameter where corneal rigidity balances tear-film surface tension) [1], [2]. Record the **time of day** of every reading, assess **inter-eye asymmetry** (>3–4 mmHg is suspicious for unilateral/asymmetric glaucoma), and consider **diurnal IOP phasing** (or repeated visits at different times) to detect early-morning or off-hour IOP spikes, especially in suspected NTG or progressing POAG [1], [2].

**Central Corneal Thickness (CCT)** should be measured by ultrasonic pachymetry at baseline evaluation [1]. Thicker corneas cause GAT to overestimate true IOP while thinner corneas cause underestimation; however, **rigid arithmetic IOP-correction formulas are discouraged** because corneal biomechanics (hysteresis) vary independently of thickness, and thin CCT itself is an independent POAG risk factor in OHTS [1], [2].

sections.heading: 4. Gonioscopy (Cornerstone Step) & Anterior Segment Imaging

blocks.text: **Gonioscopy is mandatory in every glaucoma evaluation** and is the definitive examination differentiating open-angle from angle-closure disease, as well as identifying secondary mechanisms [1], [2]. Because bright light induces pupillary constriction and artificially opens a narrow angle, initial **static (non-indentation) gonioscopy** must be performed in a **darkened room** using a **short, narrow slit beam (1–2 mm)** kept strictly away from the pupil [1], [3].

items: **Static Grading Systems:** Identify the four anterior-to-posterior landmarks (**Schwalbe's line, Trabecular meshwork, Scleral spur, Ciliary body band**) in all four quadrants using the **Shaffer system** (Grade 4 = wide open 35–45° to CBB; Grade 3 = 25–35° to SS; Grade 2 = 20° to TM, closure possible; Grade 1 = ≤10° to Schwalbe's line, closure likely; Grade 0 = closed/ITC) or the comprehensive **Spaeth system** (recording iris insertion level A–E, angular approach in degrees, peripheral iris contour—regular/steep/queer—and TM pigmentation 0–4+) [2], [4].

**Dynamic (Indentation/Compression) Gonioscopy:** Performed with a small-diameter (9 mm) 4-mirror lens (Zeiss, Posner, or Sussman) by applying gentle central corneal pressure to force aqueous into the peripheral angle [2]. If the closed angle **opens** to reveal the trabecular meshwork, the closure is **appositional** (reversible with laser iridotomy); if it **remains closed**, **peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS)** are present (synechial closure) [1], [2]. Indentation also uncovers the classic **"double-hump" sign** (peripheral iris elevation over anteriorly positioned ciliary processes separated from the central lens contour by a sulcus) diagnostic of **plateau iris configuration** [2], [4].

**ISGEO Classification of Primary Angle-Closure Disease (Foster et al.):** Based on dark-room gonioscopy, IOP, and optic nerve status, patients with **≥180° (≥2 quadrants) of iridotrabecular contact (ITC)** where the posterior pigmented trabecular meshwork is not visible are staged as: **(1) PACS (Primary Angle-Closure Suspect)**—≥180° ITC with normal IOP, no PAS, and no GON; **(2) PAC (Primary Angle Closure)**—≥180° ITC with elevated IOP and/or PAS, without GON; and **(3) PACG (Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma)**—PAC accompanied by glaucomatous optic neuropathy [3].

**Adjunctive Imaging (AS-OCT & UBM):** **Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT)** provides rapid, non-contact, dark-room quantification of angle width (AOD500, TISA500) and **lens vault**, while **ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM)** penetrates the pigmented iris epithelium to visualize retro-iridal structures, confirming **plateau iris syndrome**, iridociliary cysts, lens subluxation, or aqueous misdirection [1], [4].

sections.heading: 5. Optic Nerve Head, Structural Imaging & Visual Field Evaluation

blocks.text: Once gonioscopy confirms an open angle—or after safe **laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI)** in eyes with significant occludable angles—a **dilated stereoscopic examination** of the optic nerve head (ONH) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) is performed using slit-lamp biomicroscopy (78D/90D lens) supplemented by baseline stereoscopic disc photography [1], [2].

items: **Clinical ONH & RNFL Assessment:** Estimate optic disc size (adjusting the slit beam height), inspect the neuroretinal rim for focal notching or **ISNT rule** violation, record vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR) and inter-eye asymmetry (>0.2), search for **optic disc (Drance) hemorrhages**, **beta-zone peripapillary atrophy**, and vessel bayoneting, and inspect the peripapillary **RNFL with a red-free (green) filter** for wedge or diffuse defects [1], [4].

**Optical Coherence Tomography (SD-OCT / SS-OCT):** Quantifies **peripapillary RNFL thickness** (3.4 mm circumpapillary circle, especially inferotemporal and superotemporal sectors), **macular ganglion cell–inner plexiform layer (GCIPL/GCC)** thickness (critical in early central damage and high myopia), and **Bruch's membrane opening–minimum rim width (BMO-MRW)** [1], [2]. Always verify signal strength and segmentation quality to avoid "red disease" artifacts [1].

**Standard Automated Perimetry (SAP):** Perform white-on-white threshold perimetry using **24-2 SITA Standard or SITA Faster** (adding **10-2** or **24-2C** when macular/paracentral defects or advanced constriction are suspected) [1]. Verify reliability indices (fixation losses, false positives <15%, false negatives), evaluate the **Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT)**, **Pattern Standard Deviation (PSD)**, **Mean Deviation (MD)**, and **Visual Field Index (VFI)**, and apply **Hodapp–Parrish–Anderson minimal criteria** (cluster of ≥3 non-edge points depressed at p<5% with ≥1 at p<1% in one hemifield, GHT outside normal limits, or PSD p<5%) [1], [2]. Repeat abnormal initial fields to eliminate the learning effect and establish a reliable baseline, ensuring **structure–function concordance** between ONH/OCT loss and the corresponding hemifield defect [1].

blocks.title: Critical Clinical Pearl
blocks.text: Never dilate a patient with a shallow peripheral anterior chamber (Van Herick Grade 1–2) without first performing **dark-room gonioscopy**; if occludable angle closure is present without LPI, document the optic disc undilated (or defer dilation until after LPI) and re-check IOP after any diagnostic dilation [1], [2].

1.book: AAO BCSC Section 10: Glaucoma & AAO Preferred Practice Pattern (POAG & PACD)
1.chapter: Clinical Evaluation of the Glaucoma Patient — History, Tonometry, Gonioscopy, OCT & Perimetry
1.quote: Baseline glaucoma workup requires targeted history, refraction, pupillary RAPD check, slit-lamp examination, Goldmann applanation tonometry with CCT pachymetry, dark-room static and indentation gonioscopy, stereoscopic ONH/RNFL evaluation, quantitative OCT (RNFL/GCIPL), and reliable standard automated perimetry (24-2/10-2) confirming structure–function correlation.

2.book: Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma (7th Edition) — Allingham et al.
2.chapter: Chapters 3, 4 & 6: Tonometry, Gonioscopy, and Clinical Assessment of the Optic Nerve & Visual Field
2.quote: Van Herick peripheral AC grading is only a screening test and cannot substitute for gonioscopy. Dynamic indentation gonioscopy with a 4-mirror lens differentiates appositional closure from peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) and elicits the double-hump sign in plateau iris. Rigid CCT-based IOP correction nomograms are avoided.

3.book: Foster PJ, Buhrmann R, Quigley HA, Johnson GJ — Br J Ophthalmol 2002;86:238–242
3.chapter: The Definition and Classification of Glaucoma in Prevalence Surveys (ISGEO Classification)
3.quote: Primary angle-closure disease requires ≥180° (≥2 quadrants) of iridotrabecular contact (posterior trabecular meshwork not visible on dark-room static gonioscopy): PACS (ITC alone), PAC (ITC with elevated IOP and/or PAS without GON), and PACG (PAC accompanied by glaucomatous optic neuropathy).

4.book: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology (9th/10th Edition) — John F. Salmon
4.chapter: Chapter 11: Glaucoma — Clinical Examination, Gonioscopy Grading & Anterior Segment Imaging
4.quote: Sequelae of acute angle closure include glaucomflecken (anterior subcapsular opacities), sectoral spiral iris atrophy, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and PAS. Shaffer and Spaeth systems grade angle width and iris contour, while AS-OCT and UBM characterize lens vault and ciliary body configuration behind the iris.

mcqs.q: During dynamic indentation gonioscopy with a 4-mirror lens, an eye with a closed angle displays a peripheral iris elevation separated from the central lens bulge by an intervening furrow ('double-hump sign'). Which diagnosis does this indicate?
options: Pupillary-block primary angle closure
Plateau iris configuration
Pigment dispersion syndrome with reverse pupillary block
Cyclodialysis cleft
mcqs.explanation: On indentation gonioscopy, posteriorly displaced peripheral iris drapes over anteriorly positioned ciliary processes to produce a peripheral hump separated from the central lens hump—the classic 'double-hump' sign of plateau iris configuration.

mcqs.q: According to the ISGEO classification (Foster et al.), a patient with 270° of iridotrabecular contact on dark-room gonioscopy, an IOP of 26 mmHg, two clock-hours of PAS, and a completely normal optic disc and visual field is classified as:
options: Primary Angle-Closure Suspect (PACS)
Ocular Hypertension (OHT)
Primary Angle Closure (PAC)
Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG)
mcqs.explanation: Under ISGEO criteria, ≥180° of ITC accompanied by elevated IOP and/or PAS in the absence of glaucomatous optic neuropathy defines Primary Angle Closure (PAC); once GON is present, it becomes PACG.

mcqs.q: Why must static gonioscopy be performed in a darkened room using a short, narrow slit beam kept off the pupil?
options: To avoid light-induced miosis that pulls the peripheral iris taut and falsely widens an occludable angle
To prevent corneal epithelial dehydration from the coupling gel
To maximize the visibility of posterior embryotoxon
To induce physiologic cycloplegia and relax the ciliary body band
mcqs.explanation: Bright ambient light or illumination falling across the pupil stimulates the pupillary light reflex (miosis), pulling the peripheral iris centrally and artificially opening an angle that would otherwise be closed in dim lighting.

sections.heading: 1. Overview & Systematic '5 R's' Approach to Optic Disc Evaluation

blocks.text: **Glaucomatous optic neuropathy (GON)** is a characteristic, progressive optic neuropathy driven by retinal ganglion cell (RGC) apoptosis and axonal degeneration at the lamina cribrosa, manifesting clinically as **neuroretinal rim thinning, deepening excavation (cupping), characteristic vascular remodeling, peripapillary atrophy, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) loss** [1], [2]. Because up to **30–50% of RGC axons may be lost before repeatable defects appear on standard automated perimetry**, meticulous stereoscopic examination of the optic nerve head (ONH) is indispensable for early diagnosis [1], [2].

Clinicians systematically evaluate the ONH using the **'5 R's' mnemonic** (Spaeth / Fingeret): **(1) Scleral Ring** (to establish true disc margin and **optic disc size**—small <1.5 mm, average 1.5–2.2 mm, large >2.2 mm—because large physiological discs naturally have larger cups whereas a 0.5 cup in a small disc may signify advanced glaucoma); **(2) Neuroretinal Rim** thickness and contour; **(3) Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL)** integrity; **(4) Region of Peripapillary Atrophy (PPA)**; and **(5) Retinal and optic disc hemorrhages** [1], [2].

sections.heading: 2. Neuroretinal Rim & Excavation (Cupping) Signs

blocks.text: Loss of RGC axons preferentially affects the **superior and inferior poles** of the optic nerve head because the laminar pores in these arcuate regions are larger and contain less inter-pore connective tissue support [2], [3]. This anatomical vulnerability produces the hallmark structural signs of glaucomatous cupping:

items: **Violation of the ISNT Rule & Vertical Cup Elongation:** In a healthy disc, neuroretinal rim width typically follows the **ISNT rule** (**Inferior ≥ Superior ≥ Nasal ≥ Temporal**) [1], [3]. Preferential inferotemporal and superotemporal rim erosion breaks the ISNT hierarchy and causes **vertical elongation of the cup** (vertical cup-to-disc ratio exceeding horizontal CDR) [1], [2].

**Focal Notching & Acquired Pit of the Optic Nerve (APON):** Localized complete or near-complete erosion of the neuroretinal rim to the disc margin (most often inferotemporally) produces a sharp **polar notch** [2]. A deep, localized focal excavation of the lamina cribrosa at the rim edge constitutes an **acquired pit of the optic nerve (APON)**, classically linked to normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) and dense paracentral visual field defects threatening fixation [2], [3].

**Cup-to-Disc Asymmetry:** Inter-eye vertical cup-to-disc ratio asymmetry **>0.2** in eyes with symmetrical disc sizes occurs in fewer than 1% of normal subjects and strongly suggests glaucomatous damage [1], [3].

**Saucerization vs. Undermined ('Bean-Pot') Excavation:** Early diffuse rim thinning may present as shallow sloping **saucerization** (commonly in senile sclerotic discs), whereas advanced glaucoma excavates beneath the overhanging edge of the scleral canal to create classic **undermined or 'bean-pot' cupping** [2], [5].

**Laminar Dot Sign:** Loss of prelaminar glial and axonal tissue exposes the grey fenestrated pores of the **lamina cribrosa** at the base of the cup; progression from round pores to **slit-shaped, elongated pores** reflects severe posterior mechanical deformation [2], [3].

**Cup–Pallor Concordance:** In glaucomatous optic neuropathy, the area of excavation (defined by vessel kinking/contour) **equals or exceeds the area of pallor**, while the remaining neuroretinal rim retains a healthy pink hue; conversely, **pallor exceeding cupping** or frank rim pallor indicates a **non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy** (compressive, ischemic, hereditary, or toxic) [1], [2].

items: **Optic Disc (Drance) Splinter Hemorrhage:** A superficial, flame-shaped hemorrhage situated within the peripapillary RNFL crossing the disc border—most frequently in the **inferotemporal sector** (7–8 o'clock OD; 4–5 o'clock OS) [1], [3]. Typically transient (resolving over 4–12 weeks), a Drance hemorrhage is a highly specific hallmark of GON (especially prevalent in **NTG**) and a potent biomarker predicting **subsequent focal rim notching, new RNFL defects, and visual field progression** [1], [2].

**Bayoneting Sign:** When excavation undermines the scleral rim wall, emerging retinal vessels dive steeply beneath the overhanging rim edge, vanish briefly from view, and bend sharply twice (a Z-shaped kink) as they climb back onto the retinal surface [2], [5].
**Nasalization (Nasal Shifting) of Vessels:** Progressive temporal, superior, and inferior tissue loss leaves the central retinal vascular trunk displaced toward the nasal border of the cup [2], [5].

**Baring of Circumlinear Vessels:** Normally, fine curved circumlinear vessels hug the outer margin of the physiological cup; as the neuroretinal rim recedes outward, an empty pale gap opens between the vessel and the retreating rim—a subtle early sign of focal rim thinning [2], [3].

**Overpass (Bridging) Vessels & Arteriolar Narrowing:** Deep excavation can leave vessels suspended in mid-air across the cup (**overpass vessels**), accompanied by focal or generalized narrowing of peripapillary retinal arterioles adjacent to regions of RNFL loss [2], [3].

sections.heading: 4. Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) & Peripapillary Changes

blocks.text: A. Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) Defects

Healthy arcuate nerve fibers appear as bright, glistening silvery striations radiating from the superior and inferior poles, best appreciated clinically using **red-free (green) illumination** (short-wavelength light reflects off the superficial RNFL and is absorbed by deeper melanin) [1], [3]. Glaucomatous RNFL loss presents in two forms: **(1) Localized Wedge/Slit-like Defects**, appearing as dark, sharply demarcated arcuate bands wider than a major retinal arteriole touching the disc margin (rare in normal eyes and highly specific for GON), and **(2) Diffuse RNFL Loss**, producing generalized loss of striations so that retinal vessel walls appear unusually crisp and bare against the darker underlying RPE [1], [3].
B. Peripapillary Atrophy (PPA)
Peripapillary chorioretinal atrophy is divided clinically into two concentric zones [3]:

items: **Alpha Zone (α-PPA):** Located more peripherally; characterized by irregular RPE hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation; frequent in normal eyes and clinically non-specific [3].

**Beta Zone (β-PPA):** Located centrally, directly abutting the optic disc border; displays pale bare sclera and visible large choroidal vessels caused by **complete atrophy of the RPE and choriocapillaris** [3]. Larger β-PPA is strongly associated with GON and spatially localizes to the sector of greatest neuroretinal rim thinning and visual field loss [3]. On high-resolution OCT, conventional β-PPA is further refined into **true β-zone (Bruch's membrane present without RPE)**—strongly associated with **glaucoma**—versus **γ-zone (Bruch's membrane absent)**—strongly associated with **axial myopia** [1], [3].

sections.heading: 5. Morphologic Phenotypes (Nicolela–Drance) & Differential Diagnosis

blocks.text: Nicolela and Drance categorized glaucomatous optic discs into four distinct morphologic phenotypes with meaningful systemic and functional correlations [4]:

items: **Focal Ischemic:** Localized inferotemporal or superotemporal notching/APON with relatively intact remaining rim; strongly associated with female sex, migraine/vasospasm, Drance hemorrhages, NTG, and **dense paracentral scotomas** [4].
**Myopic Glaucomatous:** Obliquely inserted/tilted disc with a prominent temporal crescent (γ-PPA) and polar rim thinning; typically younger, myopic males [4].
**Senile Sclerotic:** Shallow, gently sloping saucerized ('moth-eaten') cup surrounded by extensive 360° β-PPA and choroidal sclerosis; elderly patients with systemic vascular/ischemic disease [4].
**Generalized Enlargement (Concentric):** Large, round, steeply excavated cup with uniform concentric rim thinning and minimal PPA; classically seen in younger patients with higher untreated IOP [4].

rows: Early central visual loss and dyschromatopsia [1]
Central/cecocentral scotoma or hemianopia respecting the **vertical meridian** [1]
Polar notching, Drance hemorrhage, β-PPA, RNFL wedge defect [2], [3]

blocks.title: Red Flags Warranting Neuroimaging
blocks.text: Obtain urgent MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast when apparent 'glaucomatous cupping' is accompanied by **neuroretinal rim pallor**, age <50 years with normal IOP, rapid visual acuity loss, dyschromatopsia, or visual field defects aligning along the **vertical meridian** [1], [5].

1.chapter: Clinical Evaluation of the Optic Nerve Head and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer
1.quote: Systematic ONH evaluation assesses disc size (scleral ring), neuroretinal rim (ISNT rule), vertical cup elongation, inter-eye asymmetry >0.2, Drance disc hemorrhages, RNFL defects (red-free light), and OCT-defined β-zone vs. γ-zone PPA. Rim pallor exceeding cupping or vertical-meridian field defects warrant neuroimaging to exclude non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

2.book: Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma (7th Edition) — Allingham et al.
2.chapter: Chapter 4: Optic Nerve Head and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer in Glaucoma
2.quote: Glaucomatous cupping features vertical elongation, focal inferotemporal/superotemporal notching, acquired pit of the optic nerve (APON), undermined bean-pot walls, laminar dot sign, vessel bayoneting, nasalization, baring of circumlinear vessels, and Drance splinter hemorrhages predicting localized progression.

3.book: Jonas JB, Budde WM, Panda-Jonas S — Surv Ophthalmol 1999;43:293–320
3.chapter: Ophthalmoscopic Evaluation of the Optic Nerve Head
3.quote: Normal neuroretinal rim follows the ISNT rule (Inferior ≥ Superior ≥ Nasal ≥ Temporal). Glaucomatous β-zone peripapillary atrophy (loss of RPE and choriocapillaris exposing sclera and choroidal vessels, with Bruch's membrane intact on OCT) spatially correlates with rim notching and visual field loss, distinct from non-specific α-zone and myopic γ-zone.

4.chapter: Various Glaucomatous Optic Nerve Appearances: Clinical Correlations
4.quote: Four glaucomatous disc phenotypes show distinct clinical correlations: focal ischemic (vasospasm, female, NTG, paracentral scotomas), myopic (tilted disc, younger males), senile sclerotic (shallow saucerized cup, marked β-PPA, elderly vascular disease), and generalized enlargement (younger patients, higher IOP).

5.book: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology (9th/10th Edition) — John F. Salmon
5.chapter: Chapter 11: Glaucoma — Optic Nerve Head Signs & Differential Diagnosis
5.quote: Characteristic vascular signs of advanced glaucomatous excavation include bayoneting of vessels over undermined rim walls, nasal shifting of the vascular trunk, overpass vessels bridging deep cups, and transient flame-shaped splinter hemorrhages at the disc margin.

mcqs.q: A 62-year-old woman with normal-tension glaucoma develops a flame-shaped Drance splinter hemorrhage at the 7 o'clock disc margin of her right eye. What is the primary clinical significance of this finding?
options: It indicates retinal vein occlusion requiring immediate anti-VEGF injection
It is a benign age-related finding unrelated to visual field stability
It strongly predicts subsequent localized neuroretinal rim notching, RNFL loss, and visual field progression
It confirms non-glaucomatous compressive optic neuropathy
mcqs.explanation: Optic disc (Drance) splinter hemorrhages—most frequently inferotemporal and common in NTG—typically resolve within 4–12 weeks but strongly predict localized focal notching, RNFL defect development, and visual field progression.

mcqs.q: On spectral-domain OCT of the peripapillary region, which subtype of peripapillary atrophy is characterized by absent RPE with an INTACT Bruch's membrane and shows the strongest association with glaucomatous optic neuropathy?
options: Alpha zone (α-PPA)
True Beta zone (β-PPA)
Gamma zone (γ-PPA)
Delta zone (δ-PPA)
mcqs.explanation: True β-zone PPA (absent RPE/choriocapillaris with intact Bruch's membrane on OCT) is strongly associated with glaucoma and spatially aligns with rim notching, whereas γ-zone (absent Bruch's membrane) is primarily linked to axial myopia.

mcqs.q: Which Nicolela–Drance glaucomatous optic disc phenotype is characterized by a shallow, gently sloping 'saucerized' cup, extensive 360° β-zone peripapillary atrophy, and strong association with elderly patients having systemic vascular disease?
options: Focal ischemic disc
Myopic glaucomatous disc
Generalized enlargement of the optic cup
Senile sclerotic disc
mcqs.explanation: The senile sclerotic phenotype presents with shallow saucerization ('moth-eaten' rim), prominent circumferential β-PPA, and choroidal sclerosis in older patients with systemic vascular/ischemic disease.

sections.heading: 1. Overview of Major Secondary Open-Angle Glaucomas

blocks.text: **Exfoliative (pseudoexfoliation) glaucoma (XFG)** and **pigmentary glaucoma (PG)** represent the two most prevalent secondary open-angle glaucomas worldwide [1], [2]. Both elevate intraocular pressure primarily through mechanical and cellular obstruction of the trabecular meshwork—by fibrillogranular extracellular matrix material in XFG and by liberated iris melanin granules in PG—yet they occupy opposite poles of the demographic, refractive, anatomical, and surgical risk spectrum [1], [2].

sections.heading: 2. Exfoliative (Pseudoexfoliation) Syndrome (XFS) & Exfoliative Glaucoma (XFG)

blocks.text: A. Epidemiology, Genetics & Pathophysiology

Exfoliation syndrome is the **most common identifiable cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma**, affecting elderly individuals (typically **>60–70 years**) with especially high prevalence in Scandinavian/Nordic, Mediterranean, Greek, and South Indian populations [1], [2]. Although clinically **markedly asymmetric** (unilateral presentation in ~50% at diagnosis), ultrastructural and histological studies confirm it is fundamentally a **bilateral** disorder that converts to bilateral involvement over time [1], [2]. Genetic susceptibility is strongly tied to coding variants in the *LOXL1* (**Lysyl Oxidase-Like 1**) gene on chromosome **15q24.1**, which encodes an enzyme required for elastin fiber cross-linking [1], [3].

Pathophysiologically, XFS is a **systemic age-related elastosis** characterized by synthesis and deposition of grey-white, fibrillogranular basement-membrane-like extracellular material across anterior segment structures (lens capsule, zonules, iris, ciliary body, trabecular meshwork, corneal endothelium) as well as systemic tissues (heart, blood vessels, meninges, lungs, skin—associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular morbidity) [1], [2]. IOP elevation results mainly from **juxtacanalicular trabecular meshwork obstruction** by exfoliation material and shed iris pigment, accompanied by trabecular endothelial degeneration and Schlemm's canal collapse; additionally, **zonular weakness** permits anterior displacement of the lens–iris diaphragm, predisposing up to 15–25% of eyes to superimposed **secondary angle closure** [1], [2].
B. Key Clinical & Gonioscopic Features

items: **Anterior Lens Capsule 'Target' (Bull's-Eye) Sign (Pathognomonic):** Best appreciated after pupillary dilation, deposits arrange into three concentric zones: (1) a translucent **central disc**, (2) a **clear intermediate zone** wiped clean by friction from the moving pupillary margin, and (3) a frosted, granular **peripheral band** with curled anterior edges [1], [5].

**Iris and Pupil Signs:** Dandruff-like white flakes along the pupillary border, **peripupillary ('moth-eaten') iris transillumination defects** due to loss of the pupillary ruff, vigorous pigment dispersion into the anterior chamber following mydriasis, and **poor pupillary dilation** resulting from stromal fibrosis and sphincter infiltration [1], [2].

**Cornea and Blood–Aqueous Barrier:** Exfoliation flakes on the corneal endothelium, reduced endothelial cell density (**PXF keratopathy**), and mild aqueous flare due to blood–aqueous barrier breakdown [2], [5].

**Gonioscopy:** **Patchy, uneven heavy hyperpigmentation** of the trabecular meshwork (densest inferiorly), a wavy pigmented band anterior to Schwalbe's line (**Sampaolesi line**), occasional exfoliation flakes in the inferior recess, and narrow angles in eyes with zonular laxity [1], [5].

**Zonular Instability & Cataract Surgery Risk:** Degeneration of zonular fibers produces **phacodonesis**, iridodonesis, and spontaneous lens subluxation; cataract surgery carries elevated risks of **zonular dialysis, posterior capsular rupture (PCR), vitreous loss, postoperative IOP spikes, and late in-the-bag IOL dislocation** (frequently necessitating iris hooks/pupil expanders and capsular tension rings) [1], [2].

blocks.text: C. Clinical Course & Management

Compared with POAG, XFG exhibits **higher baseline IOP, wider diurnal IOP fluctuations, faster optic nerve and visual field progression** (>2-fold faster progression in EMGT), and poorer long-term responsiveness to medical therapy alone [1], [2]. Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) is often highly effective initially due to abundant trabecular pigment, though its durability tends to wane sooner than in POAG and post-laser IOP spikes must be monitored [1]. Earlier progression to filtering surgery (trabeculectomy) is common, while phacoemulsification alone yields modest IOP reduction [1], [2].

sections.heading: 3. Pigment Dispersion Syndrome (PDS) & Pigmentary Glaucoma (PG)

blocks.text: A. Epidemiology, Genetics & Pathophysiology

Pigmentary glaucoma represents the glaucomatous stage of **pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS)**, classically affecting **young (20–45 years), myopic, Caucasian males** (male-to-female ratio ~2:1 in PG despite near-equal sex prevalence in PDS) [1], [2]. Familial clustering suggests autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance linked to loci including chromosome **7q35–q36** and *PMEL* variants [1], [2]. Roughly **10% of PDS eyes convert to PG within 5 years** and **15% within 15 years**, with higher conversion risk in males, high baseline IOP, and prominent Krukenberg spindles [2], [5].

According to **Campbell's mechanical rubbing theory**, a deep anterior chamber and **posteriorly bowed (concave) peripheral iris** bring the posterior iris pigment epithelium into direct mechanical contact with the **anterior packets of lens zonules** during accommodation, blinking, and pupillary excursion [4]. This concavity is maintained by **reverse pupillary block** (Karickhoff)—a one-way flap-valve effect in which blinking drives aqueous from the posterior into the anterior chamber while iridolenticular contact prevents return flow, creating higher pressure in the AC than the PC that forces the peripheral iris backward onto the zonules [2], [4]. Released melanin granules initially cause reversible **trabecular meshwork clogging** (acute IOP spikes after exercise or dilation) and subsequently induce **trabecular endothelial phagocytic overload, cell death, denudation of trabecular beams, and beam collapse**, resulting in permanent outflow obstruction [1], [4].
B. Classic Clinical & Gonioscopic Features

items: **Krukenberg Spindle:** A vertical, fusiform band of brown melanin pigment deposited on the central/inferior corneal endothelium, sculpted by aqueous thermal convection currents (Turk's line) [1], [5].

**Mid-Peripheral Radial Spoke-Like Iris Transillumination Defects (Pathognomonic):** Slit-like radial defects in the mid-peripheral iris matching the exact distribution of underlying zonular packets (unlike the peripupillary defects of XFG); accompanied by a **deep anterior chamber**, posteriorly **concave iris contour**, and fine melanin dusting on the anterior iris stroma (which may cause subtle heterochromia in asymmetric cases) [1], [4].

**Lens & Posterior Segment Signs:** Pigment deposition along the posterior lens equator at Wieger's ligament (**Zentmayer ring / Scheie's line**); notably, myopic PDS/PG eyes carry an increased incidence of **lattice degeneration and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (up to 6–7%)** [2], [5].

**Gonioscopy:** Wide-open angle (Shaffer Grade 4) with posterior iris bowing, a **dense, velvety, homogeneous 360° dark-brown band of trabecular meshwork pigmentation**, and a prominent **Sampaolesi line** [1], [5].

blocks.text: C. Natural History ('Burn-Out' Phase) & Management Pearls

Patients may experience **transient halos, blurred vision, and acute IOP spikes** following vigorous exercise or pharmacologic pupillary dilation [2]. Encouragingly, as the crystalline lens thickens with advancing age (5th–6th decade), forward lens expansion lifts the iris off the zonules, entering a **'burn-out' phase** characterized by cessation of pigment shedding, gradual clearing of inferior TM pigment (the **reversal sign**, leaving the superior TM darker than the inferior TM), and easier IOP control—sometimes mimicking normal-tension glaucoma later in life [1], [2].

blocks.title: Therapeutic & Laser Precautions in Pigmentary Glaucoma
items: **Medical Therapy:** Prostaglandin analogues and aqueous suppressants are first-line; low-dose **pilocarpine** relieves iris concavity and blocks exercise-induced IOP spikes, but is poorly tolerated in young myopes due to accommodative spasm and demands **thorough peripheral retinal examination** first because of retinal detachment risk [1], [2].

**Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI):** Equalizes AC–PC pressure and flattens reverse pupillary block on UBM/AS-OCT; most beneficial in younger PDS eyes with active concavity before irreversible TM collapse, though clinical trials have shown variable efficacy in halting conversion to PG [1], [2].

**SLT Energy Caution:** Because the heavily pigmented trabecular meshwork absorbs laser energy intensely, SLT in PG must be performed with **reduced energy settings (e.g., 0.3–0.5 mJ) and limited initial treatment (180°)** to avoid severe, prolonged post-SLT IOP spikes [1], [5].

basic-clinical_science-6.shortTitle: Role of IOP in Glaucoma Development & Progression

sections.heading: 1. Physiological IOP Distribution & Modern Conceptual Paradigm

blocks.text: In the general adult population, intraocular pressure (IOP) averages **15.5 ± 2.6 mmHg**, yielding a statistical two-standard-deviation interval of roughly **10–21 mmHg**, though the population curve is **skewed to the right** (non-Gaussian) in older adults [1], [2]. Historically, 21 mmHg was treated as an arbitrary diagnostic boundary; however, modern glaucoma epidemiology has replaced that threshold with a **continuous risk paradigm** [1], [2].

Approximately 5–10% of adults over age 40 have IOP >21 mmHg without optic nerve damage (**ocular hypertension**, the majority of whom never develop glaucoma), whereas **30–50% of patients with POAG** present with screening IOP ≤21 mmHg (**normal-tension glaucoma / NTG**) [1], [2]. Nevertheless, **IOP remains the single most important causal risk factor and the ONLY clinically proven modifiable factor** governing both the development and progression of virtually all forms of glaucoma—including OHT, high-tension POAG, NTG, PACG, and secondary glaucomas [1], [3], [4].

sections.heading: 2. Pathophysiological Mechanisms Linking IOP to Optic Nerve Damage

blocks.text: IOP damages the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) through an integrated **biomechanical and vascular cascade** centered at the optic nerve head (ONH) [1], [2]:

items: **Mechanical Strain & Translaminar Pressure Gradient (TLPG):** The **lamina cribrosa** forms the structural pressure barrier separating the intraocular compartment (IOP) from the retrolaminar subarachnoid space (**intracranial/CSF pressure, ICP**) [1], [2]. An elevated **translaminar pressure gradient** (TLPG = IOP − ICP)—whether from high IOP or abnormally low CSF pressure (as implicated in NTG)—induces circumferential hoop stress in the peripapillary sclera and **posterior bowing, compression, and shear deformation of the laminar sheets**, especially at the structurally vulnerable superior and inferior poles [1], [2].

**Axoplasmic Transport Blockade & RGC Apoptosis:** Mechanical kinking and compression of RGC axon bundles across deformed laminar pores disrupt both **orthograde and retrograde axoplasmic transport**, depriving retinal ganglion cell bodies of essential target-derived survival neurotrophins—principally **brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)**—and activating intrinsic **apoptotic pathways** [1], [2].

**Vascular Perfusion & Autoregulatory Compromise:** IOP directly opposes arterial blood entry into the optic nerve head, reducing **ocular perfusion pressure** (OPP = MAP − IOP) [2]. When elevated IOP exceeds local vascular autoregulatory reserve (or interacts with systemic hypotension/vasospasm), chronic optic nerve head ischemia, reactive astrocyte remodeling, oxidative stress, and glutamate excitotoxicity accelerate axonal loss [1], [2].

sections.heading: 3. Landmark Randomized Clinical Trial Evidence (Development & Progression)

blocks.text: Multicenter randomized controlled trials have definitively established a **direct causal relationship** between IOP reduction and protection against both glaucoma onset and visual field deterioration across the entire IOP spectrum [1], [3], [4], [5]:

rows: 5-yr POAG conversion fell from **9.5% to 4.4%** (HR 0.40; >50% RRR) [3]
Proved IOP lowering halves **development/onset** of POAG in OHT [3]
Early untreated POAG/NTG/XFG; mean **~25% IOP ↓** (~5.1 mmHg) [4]
6-yr progression fell from **62% to 45%**; **~10% lower risk per 1 mmHg ↓** (HR 0.90) [4]
Quantified continuous **dose–response** benefit across early glaucoma [4]
Proved IOP is **causally involved even in NTG** (IOP ≤21 mmHg) [5]
Advanced POAG failing medications; post-hoc IOP consistency groups [5]
Eyes with **IOP <18 mmHg at 100% of visits** (mean **12.3 mmHg**) had **~0 net VF loss** over 6–8 yrs [5]
Demonstrated that **low, consistently controlled IOP** halts advanced loss [5]
Newly diagnosed POAG; CIGTS aggressive ↓ (~35–48%); UKGTS latanoprost vs. placebo [1], [2]
CIGTS achieved minimal VF progression; UKGTS halved 24-mo VF progression (**HR 0.44**, p=0.0003) [1]
Confirmed early, sustained IOP lowering preserves visual fields [1]

sections.heading: 4. Beyond Mean IOP: Peak IOP, Diurnal & Long-Term Fluctuation

blocks.text: Although **mean IOP** is a robust predictor of progression, single daytime office readings may miss critical pressure dynamics [1], [2]:

items: **Diurnal (Short-Term) IOP Fluctuation:** Healthy eyes normally vary by **3–6 mmHg** over 24 hours, typically peaking in the **early morning or nocturnal supine hours** (driven by increased episcleral venous pressure in the recumbent posture) [1], [2]. Glaucomatous eyes frequently exhibit wider swings (**>8–10 mmHg**), and home-tonometry studies (Asrani et al.) demonstrated that large diurnal ranges independently predict visual field progression even when office IOP appears controlled [2].

**Long-Term (Inter-Visit) IOP Fluctuation & Peak IOP:** In **AGIS**, greater inter-visit IOP standard deviation (**>3 mmHg**) predicted visual field deterioration independently of mean IOP (particularly among patients with lower mean IOPs), and **CIGTS** linked higher peak IOP and range to progression in medically treated eyes [2], [5]. Conversely, **EMGT** found mean follow-up IOP—rather than inter-visit fluctuation—to be the dominant determinant in early disease [4]. Collectively, clinicians aim to control **mean IOP, peak IOP, and fluctuation** simultaneously [1], [2].

sections.heading: 5. Clinical Translation: Setting & Dynamically Adjusting Target IOP

blocks.text: Because susceptibility to IOP varies dramatically among individuals, management is guided by an individualized **Target IOP**—defined as an upper IOP threshold estimated to prevent further structural or functional damage that would impair vision-related quality of life over the patient's expected lifetime [1], [2].

items: **Severity-Stratified Initial Targets:** As a practical fellowship framework, initial target IOP typically aims for **20–30% reduction** (often high teens) in mild glaucoma, **30–40% reduction** (mid-teens) in moderate glaucoma, and **≥40% reduction** (often **low teens, 10–14 mmHg**, guided by AGIS) in severe or advanced disease [1], [2].

**Baseline Untreated IOP & Life Expectancy:** Eyes sustaining optic nerve damage at low untreated pressures (NTG) demand a deeper percentage drop (at least **≥30%** per CNTGS), and younger patients with longer life expectancy or monocular status warrant stricter targets [1], [5].

**Dynamic Re-Evaluation:** Target IOP is never fixed; if confirmed structural (OCT) or functional (SAP) progression occurs despite achieving office target IOP, clinicians must verify medication adherence, evaluate occult nocturnal/diurnal peaks, and **reset the target IOP lower** (escalating medical, laser, or surgical therapy) [1], [2].

blocks.title: Exam Synthesis Pearl
blocks.text: Always remember the four pillars of IOP evidence for FAICO exams: **OHTS** (≥20% ↓ halves *conversion* from 9.5% to 4.4%), **EMGT** (~10% lower *progression* per 1 mmHg ↓), **CNTGS** (≥30% ↓ cuts *NTG progression* from 35% to 12%), and **AGIS** (IOP <18 mmHg at 100% of visits, mean 12.3 mmHg, yields near-zero *advanced* VF loss) [3], [4], [5].

sections.heading: 1. Physiological Basis, Normal Distribution & the Modified Goldmann Equation

blocks.text: Intraocular pressure (IOP) is the fluid pressure exerted by the ocular contents against the corneoscleral envelope, maintained dynamically by the equilibrium between aqueous humor production and aqueous humor drainage against episcleral venous back-pressure [1]. Population-based epidemiological studies demonstrate a mean adult IOP of approximately **15.5 ± 2.6 mmHg**, defining a statistical normal range of **10–21 mmHg** (mean ± 2 SD), although the population distribution is **non-Gaussian and skewed to the right** toward higher pressures, particularly after 40 years of age [1][2].
Modified Goldmann Equation:   IOP = (F − U) / C + Pv   [1]

In this governing physiological relationship, **F** represents the rate of aqueous humor formation (normal **2.0–2.5 µL/min**), **U** denotes pressure-independent uveoscleral outflow (accounting for **10–20%** of total outflow in older adults and higher in younger eyes), **C** denotes conventional trabecular outflow facility (normal **0.25–0.30 µL/min/mmHg**), and **Pv** represents episcleral venous pressure (normal **8–10 mmHg**) [1][2]. Nearly every physiological, ocular, systemic, or pharmacological factor alters IOP either by modulating one of these four variables or by applying external mechanical compression to the globe [1][2].

sections.heading: 2. Demographic, Genetic & Circadian Factors

items: **Age:** In Western epidemiological cohorts (such as the Baltimore, Beaver Dam, and Blue Mountains Eye Studies), mean IOP rises subtly with advancing age because progressive age-related declines in trabecular outflow facility (**C**) and uveoscleral outflow (**U**) outweigh the modest ~2.4% per decade reduction in aqueous humor formation (**F**) [1][2]. Conversely, in some East Asian cohorts (such as the Tajimi Study), cross-sectional IOP remains stable or declines slightly with age due to cohort differences in body mass index and systemic blood pressure [2].

**Race and Ethnicity:** Individuals of African descent exhibit slightly higher mean IOP (and thinner average central corneal thickness) than European populations, whereas East Asian populations generally demonstrate lower mean IOP with a higher proportion of normal-tension glaucoma [1][2].

**Sex and Hormonal Status:** Gender differences are minimal between ages 20 and 40 years, but postmenopausal women show a modest elevation in IOP (~0.5–1.0 mmHg) associated with estrogen decline, whereas pregnancy—especially the third trimester—is associated with a physiological **10–20% reduction in IOP** mediated by elevated progesterone and relaxin increasing outflow facility [2][3].

**Heredity:** Intraocular pressure displays polygenic inheritance; first-degree relatives of patients with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) show higher mean baseline IOP and a higher prevalence of corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension [2].

**Circadian (Diurnal and Nocturnal) Rhythm:** Normal eyes exhibit a physiological 24-hour fluctuation of **2–6 mmHg**, whereas glaucomatous eyes characteristically show exaggerated diurnal swings exceeding **8–10 mmHg** [1][3]. Under classic daytime seated measurements, IOP typically peaks in the early morning shortly after awakening and reaches a trough in the late afternoon; however, 24-hour habitual-position sleep-laboratory studies demonstrate that **true peak IOP occurs during the nocturnal supine period**, driven by recumbent elevation of episcleral venous pressure (**Pv**) despite a ~45% nocturnal suppression of aqueous production (**F**) [4].

**Seasonal Variation:** Population measurements demonstrate slightly higher IOP during winter months compared with summer months, likely linked to seasonal fluctuations in ambient light exposure, hormonal balance, and systemic vascular tone [2].

sections.heading: 3. Local Ocular Factors

items: **Refractive Error and Axial Length:** High axial myopia is associated with a slightly higher mean IOP, increased susceptibility to corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension, and greater vulnerability of the optic nerve head to pressure-mediated axonal injury [2].

**Accommodation and Pupillary Dynamics:** Contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle (Brücke's muscle) during accommodation pulls the scleral spur posteriorly, widening the intertrabecular pores (**↑C**) and lowering IOP by **2–4 mmHg** [2][3]. Conversely, pharmacological or physiological mid-mydriasis in anatomically narrow angles precipitates pupillary block and acute IOP elevation [1].

**Blinking, Eyelid Squeezing, and Extraocular Muscle Tone:** Normal gentle blinking transiently raises IOP by **5–10 mmHg**, whereas forceful blepharospasm or eyelid squeezing during examination can spike IOP dramatically by **50–90 mmHg** through direct orbicularis compression [2][3]. Gaze into the field of a fibrotic or restricted extraocular muscle (notably in **thyroid eye disease** during upgaze) causes marked transient IOP elevation due to globe indentation by the tethered inferior rectus (**Braley's sign**) [2].

**Ocular Inflammation and Anterior Segment Pathology:** Anterior uveitis exerts a dual effect—it can **lower IOP** via ciliary body inflammation and reduced aqueous secretion (**↓F**), or **elevate IOP** via trabeculitis, inflammatory debris/fibrin obstructing the trabecular meshwork (**↓C**), peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), or steroid response [1][2]. Pigment release, pseudoexfoliative material, red blood cells, ghost cells, and lens protein similarly elevate IOP by reducing trabecular facility [1].

**Corneal Biomechanics (Measurement Artifact vs. True IOP):** Central corneal thickness (CCT) and corneal hysteresis do not alter true intracameral pressure, but they substantially influence *measured* applanation IOP and must always be differentiated from true physiological IOP change [1].

sections.heading: 4. Systemic, Postural, Mechanical & Lifestyle Factors

items: **Body Posture and Inversion:** Transitioning from a sitting/upright posture to a supine position elevates IOP by **2–6 mmHg** (often greater in glaucomatous eyes) via hydrostatic elevation of **Pv** and choroidal vascular engorgement [2][4]. Extreme head-down positioning—such as Trendelenburg surgical positioning or yoga headstands (*Sirsasana*)—can double IOP (elevations of **20–40 mmHg**) and poses a documented risk for glaucomatous progression [4].

**Valsalva Maneuver and Venous Obstruction:** Heavy weightlifting with breath-holding, playing high-resistance wind instruments (e.g., trumpet or oboe), coughing, vomiting, or wearing an overly tight necktie impedes internal jugular venous return, rapidly raising **Pv** and generating acute IOP spikes exceeding **30–45 mmHg** [2][4].

**Exercise:** Acute **dynamic aerobic exercise** (running, cycling) transiently lowers IOP by **2–6 mmHg** for 30–60 minutes through systemic lactic acidosis, hypocapnia, and increased plasma osmolarity drawing fluid out of the globe [2][4]. In contrast, **isometric resistance exercise** accompanied by a Valsalva maneuver acutely raises IOP [4].

**Systemic Hemodynamics and Metabolic Conditions:** Systemic systolic blood pressure correlates positively with IOP (approximately **+0.2 to +0.3 mmHg** per 10 mmHg rise in systolic BP), while obesity, diabetes mellitus, and obstructive sleep apnea are associated with mildly elevated baseline IOP [1][2]. Pathological elevation of episcleral venous pressure occurs in **carotid–cavernous fistula**, dural arteriovenous malformations, **Sturge–Weber syndrome**, thyroid orbitopathy, and superior vena cava obstruction [1][2].

**Fluid Loading, Caffeine, Alcohol, and Smoking:** Rapid ingestion of hypotonic water (800–1000 mL within 5 minutes, as in the **water-drinking test**) lowers plasma osmolarity and induces choroidal engorgement, producing an acute IOP spike in eyes with impaired outflow facility [3]. **Caffeine** transiently elevates IOP by **1–3 mmHg** for 1–2 hours (especially in OAG/OHT) via phosphodiesterase inhibition and increased intracellular cAMP, whereas **ethanol (alcohol)** transiently lowers IOP via hyperosmotic diuresis and inhibition of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) [2][4]. Tobacco smoking causes brief acute IOP elevation [2].

sections.heading: 5. Pharmacological & Anesthetic Factors Affecting IOP

blocks.text: Systemic, topical, and anesthetic drugs exert potent, clinically critical effects on intraocular pressure that directly influence glaucoma diagnosis, medical management, and ophthalmic surgery [1][2].

rows: Inhibits trabecular phagocytosis, increases ECM/GAG & myocilin deposition → **↓↓C** [1][2].
Precipitates pupillary block in narrow angles; mild ciliary relaxation reduces **C** in some POAG [2].
Idiosyncratic ciliochoroidal effusion → anterior rotation of lens–iris diaphragm (secondary angle closure) [1].
Tonic contraction of extraocular muscles (succinylcholine) and sympathetic tone/EOM tension (ketamine) [2][4].
Central hypothalamic depression, EOM relaxation, and reduced systemic BP/Pv (important during pediatric EUA!) [2][4].
Creates blood–ocular osmotic gradient drawing water out of the vitreous cavity [1].
**Antiglaucoma Agents** (PGAs, β-blockers, α2-agonists, CAIs, ROCK inhibitors, miotics)
Reduce **F** (β-blockers, CAIs, α2), increase **U** (PGAs, α2), or enhance **C** (miotics, ROCK inhibitors) [1].

blocks.title: Clinical Correlation — Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) in Pediatric Glaucoma
blocks.text: Most general anesthetics (especially **sevoflurane, isoflurane, halothane, and propofol**) artificially **lower IOP**, potentially masking congenital glaucoma; conversely, **ketamine** and **succinylcholine** transiently raise IOP [2][4]. During pediatric EUA, IOP should ideally be measured as early as possible after gentle induction (before endotracheal intubation) using handheld tonometry (Perkins, iCare, or Tono-Pen) and interpreted alongside corneal diameter, Haab striae, axial length, and optic disc cupping [2][4].

1.chapter: Chapter 2: Intraocular Pressure and Aqueous Humor Dynamics
1.quote: Mean adult IOP is ~15.5 ± 2.6 mmHg (10–21 mmHg) with a right-skewed distribution. Modified Goldmann equation: IOP = (F − U)/C + Pv (F = 2.0–2.5 µL/min, C = 0.25–0.30 µL/min/mmHg, Pv = 8–10 mmHg). Corticosteroids reduce C; topiramate causes ciliochoroidal effusion and bilateral angle closure.

2.book: Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma (7th Edition) — Allingham et al.
2.quote: Factors influencing IOP include age, race, heredity, refractive error, accommodation (lowers IOP via longitudinal ciliary muscle pull on scleral spur), eyelid squeezing (+50–90 mmHg), restrictive EOM (thyroid eye disease), supine/inverted posture, Valsalva, aerobic exercise (lowers IOP), caffeine, alcohol, and anesthetic agents.

3.book: Becker-Shaffer's Diagnosis and Therapy of the Glaucomas (8th Edition)
3.chapter: Chapter 5: Intraocular Pressure and Its Regulation
3.quote: Normal diurnal IOP fluctuation is 2–6 mmHg, whereas glaucomatous eyes frequently fluctuate >8–10 mmHg. Pregnancy reduces IOP by 10–20% in the third trimester via hormonal enhancement of outflow facility; water-drinking induces transient IOP spikes in eyes with compromised outflow facility.

4.book: Liu JHK et al., IOVS / Ophthalmology (1998–2003) & Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology (9th Edition)
4.chapter: 24-Hour Habitual-Position IOP Rhythm, Posture & Systemic Pharmacological Effects
4.quote: Sleep-laboratory 24-hour monitoring demonstrates nocturnal IOP elevation in the habitual supine posture due to increased episcleral venous pressure despite ~45% nocturnal reduction in aqueous production. Head-down postures (Sirsasana), isometric Valsalva, succinylcholine, and ketamine elevate IOP, whereas volatile anesthetics and propofol lower IOP.

mcqs.q: Despite an approximately 45% physiological reduction in aqueous humor formation during sleep, why does 24-hour habitual-position monitoring reveal the highest IOP during the nocturnal period?
options: Nocturnal sympathetic surge dramatically increases episcleral arterial inflow
Supine body posture elevates episcleral venous pressure (Pv) and choroidal vascular engorgement
Nocturnal miosis completely blocks conventional trabecular outflow
Overnight corneal edema artificially doubles true intracameral pressure
mcqs.explanation: In the habitual supine sleeping posture, hydrostatic elevation of episcleral venous pressure (Pv) and choroidal venous engorgement outweigh the nocturnal ~45% decline in aqueous production, producing peak 24-hour IOP at night.

mcqs.q: Which of the following physiological or pharmacological maneuvers reliably produces a transient DECREASE in intraocular pressure?
options: Isometric weightlifting performed with a Valsalva maneuver
Administration of intravenous succinylcholine prior to intubation
Sustained accommodation and dynamic aerobic exercise
Yoga headstand (Sirsasana) positioning
mcqs.explanation: Accommodation pulls the scleral spur posteriorly via longitudinal ciliary muscle contraction (increasing trabecular facility C), and dynamic aerobic exercise raises plasma osmolarity and induces lactic acidosis/hypocapnia—both transiently lowering IOP.

mcqs.q: According to the modified Goldmann equation IOP = (F − U)/C + Pv, corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension raises IOP primarily by altering which parameter?
options: Decreasing conventional trabecular outflow facility (C)
Increasing aqueous humor secretion rate (F)
Increasing episcleral venous pressure (Pv)
Eliminating pressure-independent uveoscleral outflow (U)
mcqs.explanation: Corticosteroids reduce trabecular outflow facility (C) by inhibiting trabecular endothelial phagocytosis and promoting accumulation of extracellular matrix, glycosaminoglycans, and myocilin within the juxtacanalicular meshwork.

basic-clinical_science-8.shortTitle: Principles & Technique of Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction & Physical Basis (The Imbert–Fick Law)

blocks.text: Introduced by Hans Goldmann and Theo Schmidt in 1954–1957, **Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT)** is a variable-force, constant-area applanation technique that remains the international clinical reference standard for intraocular pressure measurement and the benchmark used in landmark randomized glaucoma trials (OHTS, EMGT, AGIS, CIGTS) [1][2].

GAT is grounded in the **Imbert–Fick Law**, which states that for an ideal, dry, infinitely thin, perfectly flexible elastic sphere, the internal pressure (**P**) equals the external flattening force (**W**) divided by the applanated surface area (**A**) [1][2]:
Ideal Imbert–Fick Law:   P = W / A     |     Goldmann Modification:   W + M = (P × A) + S   [1][2]

Because the human cornea is neither infinitely thin nor dry, two opposing non-ideal forces act during corneal flattening: (1) **corneal bending rigidity (S)**, an outward structural resistance that opposes flattening and tends to overestimate IOP, and (2) **capillary surface tension of the precorneal tear film (M)**, an inward adhesive attraction pulling the prism toward the cornea that tends to underestimate IOP [1][2].

Goldmann and Schmidt empirically determined in human cadaver eyes (assuming a normal central corneal thickness of **~520 µm**) that at an exact applanation diameter of **3.06 mm** (applanation area **A = π × (1.53)² = 7.354 mm²**), three remarkable physical advantages occur simultaneously [1][2]:

items: **Cancellation of Non-Ideal Forces:** Corneal bending resistance (**S**) and tear-film capillary attraction (**M**) precisely balance and cancel each other (**S ≈ M**), simplifying the relationship back to **P = W / A** [1][2].
**Direct Linear Conversion:** An applied force of **0.1 gram-force** produces exactly **1 mmHg** (so a dial force of **1.0 gram = 10 mmHg**, as 1 g / 7.354 mm² = 0.136 g/mm² = 10 mmHg) [1][2].

**Independence from Ocular Rigidity:** Applanating a 3.06 mm disc displaces only **~0.56 µL** of aqueous humor, raising true IOP by merely **~2.5–3%** during contact—making GAT virtually independent of **scleral (ocular) rigidity**, unlike Schiøtz indentation tonometry (which displaces 15–20 µL) [1][2].

sections.heading: 2. Optical Design of the Biprism & Clinical Technique

blocks.text: The Goldmann tonometer head consists of a transparent plastic truncated cone (7.0 mm outer diameter) housing a **split optical biprism** mounted apex-to-base within its core [2]. This biprism splits the circular fluorescein-stained tear meniscus at the circumference of corneal contact into two semicircular arcs (**mires**) and displaces them horizontally in opposite directions by exactly **3.06 mm** [1][2].

items: **Preparation:** Instill a drop of topical anesthetic (e.g., proparacaine 0.5%) combined with a controlled amount of sodium fluorescein (0.25% solution or moistened strip); ensure the patient loosens tight collars, rests chin and forehead firmly on the slit lamp, breathes normally, and avoids breath-holding or eyelid squeezing [1][2].

**Slit-Lamp Alignment:** Set the cobalt-blue filter (~490 nm excitation emitting ~520 nm green fluorescence) with maximal illumination and widest slit beam angled approximately **60°** temporally (or nasally) to evenly illuminate the prism tip; set the tension drum initially to **10 mmHg** (dial setting 1.0) [2][3].

**Corneal Contact & Centering:** Gently advance the slit lamp until the prism tip lightly contacts the central corneal apex (a bright limbal blue glow indicates contact). View monocularly through the aligned ocular and center the joystick vertically and horizontally until the two fluorescent semicircles are **equal in size** and symmetrical across the horizontal dividing line [2][3].

**Endpoint & Pulse Averaging:** Rotate the tension dial until the **inner margins** of the upper and lower semicircular mires **just touch (kiss)**—specifically at the **midpoint of their rhythmic ocular pulse excursion**—and multiply the dial reading (in grams) by **10** to obtain IOP in mmHg [1][2].

sections.heading: 3. Sources of Measurement Error & Astigmatism Correction

blocks.text: Accurate fellowship-level tonometry requires immediate recognition of systematic errors that shift the measured GAT reading above or below true intracameral pressure [1][3].

rows: **Excess fluorescein** → overly thick mires (>0.3 mm) shift inner edge inward, requiring higher force [1][2].
**Insufficient fluorescein** → thin, faint mires mask the true inner meniscus margin [1][2].
**Thick central cornea** (>550 µm) or dense **corneal scarring** increases bending resistance (**S**) [1][4].
**Thin cornea** (<520 µm), **post-LASIK/PRK** ablation, or **corneal edema** (spongy stroma resists less despite high pachymetry!) [1][4].
**Steep cornea** (~1 mmHg per 3 D steeper) or **against-the-rule astigmatism** (>3 D, prism horizontal) [2][3].
**Flat cornea** or **with-the-rule astigmatism** (>3 D, prism horizontal) [2][3].
Lid squeezing, examiner pressing globe while retracting lids, Valsalva/breath-holding, tight collar [1][2].
Prolonged or repeated applanation (**tonographic aqueous massage effect**), uncalibrated weak spring [2][3].

blocks.text: Management of Regular Corneal Astigmatism (>3.00 D)

Because an astigmatic cornea flattens into an ellipse rather than a circle, regular corneal astigmatism exceeding **3.00 diopters** introduces approximately **1 mmHg error per 4 diopters** of cylinder [2][3]. Two validated correction methods are used clinically: (1) rotate the biprism so that the **red alignment mark (at 43°)** on the prism holder aligns with the **axis of the negative (minus) cylinder** (the flattest corneal meridian), where the applanated elliptical area equals the standard 7.354 mm² circle; or (2) obtain two readings—one with the prism horizontal (0°) and one vertical (90°)—and **average the two measurements** [2][3].

blocks.title: OHTS & Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) Caveat
blocks.text: In the **Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)**, thinner CCT was the strongest independent baseline predictor of progression from ocular hypertension to POAG (hazard ratio **1.71 per 40 µm thinner cornea**) [4]. However, applying rigid linear CCT correction nomograms (e.g., adding/subtracting fixed mmHg per 10 µm) is **clinically discouraged** because corneal biomechanical stiffness and viscoelasticity vary independently of thickness and can introduce new inaccuracies [1][4].

sections.heading: 4. Calibration Verification & Prism Disinfection

items: **Calibration Check:** Mechanical calibration of the Goldmann counterbalanced arm should be verified monthly using the manufacturer's **calibration weight bar** at three standard dial checkpoints: **0 mmHg** (dial 0), **20 mmHg** (dial 2), and **60 mmHg** (dial 6) [1][3]. At each notch, rotating the drum slightly above or below the target mark must cause the arm to rock smoothly forward or backward within an acceptable tolerance of **±0.5 to ±1.0 mmHg** (otherwise factory recalibration is mandatory) [1][3].

**Infection Control & Prism Disinfection:** Because reusable GAT prisms contact the tear film and can transmit **adenovirus (EKC), HSV, HIV, and HBV**, the AAO and CDC recommend soaking the prism tip in **1:10 diluted sodium hypochlorite (bleach, ~5000 ppm)** for **5–10 minutes** (or 3% hydrogen peroxide), followed by thorough rinsing with sterile water/saline and complete air-drying to prevent toxic corneal epithelial injury [1][3]. Alcohol-only wipes are insufficient against non-enveloped viruses (adenovirus) and accelerate degradation of prism cement; **single-use disposable prisms** are recommended in suspected epidemic keratoconjunctivitis or prion (CJD) exposure [1][3].

1.chapter: Chapter 2: Clinical Measurement of Intraocular Pressure — Goldmann Applanation Tonometry
1.quote: GAT relies on the modified Imbert–Fick law (W + M = P·A + S). At a 3.06 mm applanation diameter (area 7.354 mm², displaced volume ~0.56 µL), tear capillary pull cancels corneal rigidity and 0.1 g equals 1 mmHg. Calibration is checked at 0, 20, and 60 mmHg; 1:10 bleach soak is recommended for prism disinfection.

2.chapter: Chapter 3: Intraocular Pressure and Tonometry — Goldmann Applanation
2.quote: The Goldmann biprism splits the fluorescein ring by 3.06 mm. Separated mires indicate the dial is too low (turn up); overlapping mires indicate the dial is too high (turn down). Excess fluorescein causes falsely high readings; insufficient fluorescein causes falsely low readings. For >3 D astigmatism, align the red 43° mark with the minus cylinder axis or average 0° and 90° readings.

3.chapter: Chapter 11: Glaucoma — Tonometry & Sources of Error
3.quote: Corneal edema yields falsely low GAT despite increased pachymetry because edematous stroma offers reduced resistance. Repeated applanation lowers IOP via aqueous massage. Calibration checks at dial settings 0, 2, and 6 (0, 20, 60 mmHg) should fall within ±0.5–1.0 mmHg.
